summary: Pammon (Ancient Greek: Πάμμων) is a Trojan prince, son of King Priam and Hecuba. Homer names him among the sons Priam rebukes when preparing Hector's ransom; Apollodorus lists him among Hecuba's children. Later epic has him command after Hector's death and fall to Neoptolemus at Troy's sack.

sections.heading: Son of Priam and Hecuba
paragraphs: In Apollodorus' Bibliotheca Priam has nine sons and four daughters by Hecuba; Pammon stands with Hector, Paris, Deiphobus, Helenus, Polites, Antiphus, Hipponous, and Polydorus among the legitimate sons, beside Creusa, Laodice, Polyxena, and Cassandra.

Homer brings him into the living drama of Book 24: when Priam resolves to go to the Achaean ships for Hector's body, he calls aloud to nine sons — including Pammon with Helenus, Paris, Agathon, Antiphonus, Polites, Deiphobus, Hippothous, and Dius — and scolds them as base children who are his shame.

sections.heading: Later tradition
paragraphs: Quintus of Smyrna's Posthomerica makes Pammon one of the commanders chosen with Alexander, Aeneas, Polydamas, Deiphobus, and others to lead the Trojan host after Hector's death. During an attack his charioteer Hippasides is killed and Pammon is forced to flee; at the fall of Troy he dies with Polites and Antiphonus at the hands of Neoptolemus, Achilles' son.
